‘Well, Jup,’ I asked, ‘what is wrong now? How does your master fare?’

‘Why, to tell de troof, massa, he ain’t quite so well as he might be.’

‘Unwell! I am very sorry to hear that. What complaint has he?’

‘Dere now! Dat’s just it—he don’t complain ob a ting, but he’s mighty sick all de same.’

‘Mighty sick, Jupiter? Why not tell me immediately? Is he obliged to keep his bed?’

‘No, dat he ain’t! He won’t keep nowheres—dat’s where de trouble lies. I got a powerful heavy mind about poor Massa Will.’

‘Jupiter, I wish I could understand you. You tell me your master is ill. Has he not explained what troubles him?’

‘Why, massa, dere ain’t no call to get angry. Massa Will says dere’s noffin wrong wid him at all. But why’s he walking round like dis, his head hanging and his shoulders up, pale as a ghost? An’ he’s always a-syphoning—’

‘Always doing what, Jupiter?’

‘A-syphoning, wid figures on de slate—de strangest figures I ever seen. I’m getting frightened, I tell you. Got to watch his doings mighty close. De other day he slipped past me before sunrise and stayed away de whole blessed day. I cut a great stick ready to give him a proper beating when he came back, but I’m such a fool I couldn’t find de heart after all—he looked so dreadful poorly.’

‘Eh? What? Ah, yes! On the whole, I should advise you not to treat the poor fellow too harshly. Do not thrash him, Jupiter; he is hardly equal to it. But have you no notion what brought on this illness, or rather this alteration in his behaviour? Has anything disagreeable occurred since I last saw you?’

‘No, massa, noffin disagreeable since den. It was before, I’m afraid—de very day you was dere.’

‘How so? What are you suggesting?’

‘Why, massa, I’m talking about de bug—dere!’

‘The what?’

‘De bug. I’m mighty certain dat gold bug bit Massa Will somewhere round his head.’

‘And what cause, Jupiter, have you for believing that?’

‘Claws enough, massa, an’ a mouth besides. Never did I see such a wicked bug—he kicks and bites whatever gets near him. Massa Will caught him first, but mighty soon had to let him loose again, I tell you. Dat must be when he got bitten. I didn’t fancy de look ob dat bug’s mouth myself, nohow, so I wouldn’t pick him up wid my fingers. I caught him in a piece ob paper I found.’

But no, something even more dazzling was possible. He would become a pirate! That was the answer! Now his future opened clearly before him, shining with unimaginable glory. His name would spread across the world and send a shiver through everyone who heard it. How magnificently he would cut through the dancing seas in his long, low, black-hulled speedster, the Spirit of the Storm, its dreadful flag flying at the bow! And at the height of his fame, he would suddenly return to the old village and stride into church, tanned and weather-beaten, wearing his black velvet doublet and breeches, enormous riding boots, crimson sash, a belt bristling with cavalry pistols, a cutlass rusted with crime at his side, and a broad-brimmed hat with waving feathers. His black skull-and-crossbones flag would be unfurled, and he would swell with delight at the whispers: ‘It’s Tom Sawyer the Pirate—the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!’

Yes, that settled it. His career was chosen. He would leave home and begin it, starting the very next morning. He must therefore make his preparations immediately and gather his resources. Going to a nearby rotten log, he began digging beneath one end with his Barlow knife. Before long he struck wood that sounded hollow. He placed his hand there and solemnly pronounced this spell:

‘Whatever has not come here, come! Whatever is here, remain!’

He then scraped away the earth and uncovered a pine shingle. Lifting it revealed a neat little treasure chamber, its sides and floor also made of shingles. A marble lay inside. Tom was utterly astonished. Scratching his head in bewilderment, he said:

‘Well, that beats everything!’

He threw the marble away irritably and stood thinking. One of the superstitions he and his companions had always considered completely reliable had failed him. If you buried a marble while reciting the necessary spells, left it untouched for two weeks, and then opened its hiding place with the words he had just spoken, every marble you had ever lost would have gathered there, however far apart they had been scattered. Yet this time the method had unquestionably failed. Tom’s entire faith shook to its foundations. He had often heard of its success, but never before of its failure. He did not remember that he himself had tried it several times already and had simply been unable to locate the hiding places afterwards. He puzzled over the problem for a while, then concluded that some witch must have interfered and broken the spell.

They were her life, dearer than any place sanctified by love, dearer than everything else the earth possessed. The boys greeted our planned departure with childish excitement. Clara asked whether we would go to Athens. ‘It is possible,’ I replied, and pleasure illuminated her face. There she would see her parents’ tomb and the country filled with memories of her father’s glory. Silently and ceaselessly she had dwelt on those scenes. Remembering them had transformed her early gaiety into seriousness and stirred ambitious, restless thoughts within her.

There were many cherished friends we could not abandon, humble creatures though they were: the spirited, obedient horse Lord Raymond had given his daughter, Alfred’s dog, and a pet eagle whose eyes had grown dim with age. Yet listing the favourites that would accompany us brought grief for our heavy losses, and deep sighs for all we must leave. Tears sprang to Idris’s eyes as Alfred and Evelyn presented first a beloved rose tree, then an exquisitely carved marble vase, insisting that these must be taken too. They lamented that we could not carry away the castle and forest, the deer and birds, and every familiar, treasured object. ‘My loving, foolish children,’ I said, ‘we have lost forever treasures far more precious than these. We abandon these things to protect treasures beside which they count for nothing. Let us never forget our purpose and our hope: they will build an unbreakable barrier against the overflowing sorrow we feel for trifles.’

The children were soon diverted and returned to imagining the pleasures ahead. Idris had disappeared. She had gone to conceal her weakness, escaping from the castle to the little park below, where she sought solitude and freedom to weep. I found her clinging to an ancient oak, pressing her rosy lips against its rough bark. Tears streamed down her face, and she could not restrain her sobs and broken cries. To see the woman so dear to my heart overwhelmed by sorrow filled me with the deepest grief. I drew her toward me. As she felt my kisses on her eyelids and the pressure of my arms, she became conscious once more of everything that remained to her. ‘You are very kind not to reproach me,’ she said. ‘I am weeping, and a bitter stab of unbearable sorrow tears my heart. Yet I am happy. Mothers mourn their children, wives lose their husbands, while I still have you and my children.’
